# Wealth as productivity; sustained economic growth (`economic_growth_productivity`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by division_of_labour, compound_interest_exponential_growth, positive_sum_cooperation, systematic_invention
- Core idea: A nation's wealth is what its people can produce and consume per head, not the gold and silver it holds. Output per worker rises with better tools and machines, more energy (water, wind, coal), skills, specialisation, trade and better organisation, and new knowledge keeps the process going. Small rates compound: 2 % a year doubles income in 35 years. The convincing comparison is 16th-century Spain, which received American silver and grew poorer, against the Dutch Republic, which had no mines and grew rich by shipping, trade and manufactures.
- Pitfalls:
  - Mercantilism: hoarding bullion and forcing export surpluses as the goal of policy
  - Zero-sum thinking: assuming one man's or nation's gain must be another's loss
  - Dismissing Malthus too quickly: for most of history, gains in output were eaten by population growth; only continuous innovation broke the trap after about 1800
  - Confusing rising money income with rising real income
  - Promising growth from one invention without the institutions, energy and markets that let it spread
- History: china: Song period (960–1279) – rapid growth of trade, cities, money and iron output; whether it raised income per head is debated; islamic: 1377 – Ibn Khaldun argues that a city's wealth comes from its people's labour and cooperation, and that heavy taxation shrinks it; europe: 1690s – Petty's political arithmetic estimates national income; 1776 Smith's Wealth of Nations against mercantilism; 1798 Malthus; c. 1800–1830 sustained growth of income per head begins in Britain and the Netherlands; global: since 1820 – world income per head has risen more than tenfold (Maddison's estimates)
- Read:
  - Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776)
  - Joel Mokyr, The Lever of Riches (1990)
  - Angus Maddison, Contours of the World Economy, 1–2030 AD (2007)
